analysis.one_liner: Restores consumers' rights to copy, transfer, and resell digital music, movies, and books they bought.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee from May 2003 until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The BALANCE Act would have amended federal copyright law to protect people who legally buy digital music, movies, and books. It would let consumers make personal backup copies, move a purchased song or movie onto any device they choose, resell a digital copy to one buyer, and — when a copyright owner refuses to provide a reasonable way to make a legitimate use — legally bypass digital locks (DRM) that prevent it. It would also void nonnegotiable license terms that strip away these rights. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers of digital entertainment: people who legally buy songs, movies, and e-books would regain rights long taken for granted with physical media — making backups, playing purchases on any device, and reselling a copy they no longer want. Device makers and technology companies would also gain freedom to build products that play or transfer digital works without fear of lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Buyers of digital music, movies, and e-books

how_it_helps.text: It would make clear that fair use applies to digital transmissions, so copying a legally acquired digital work for personal, non-public use is not infringement [S2][S3].

It would create a 'digital first sale' right: the owner of a digital copy could sell or transfer it to a single recipient, so long as they do not keep a retrievable copy and the work stays in its original format [S2][S3].

It would allow bypassing DRM encryption when needed to make a legitimate (noninfringing) use, but only if the copyright owner fails to provide a way to make that use without added cost or burden to the consumer [S2][S3].
It would override nonnegotiable license terms — like click-through agreements — that purport to strip consumers of these fair-use and first-sale rights [S3].

The bill's stated purpose was to 'safeguard the rights and expectations of consumers who lawfully obtain digital entertainment,' citing court rulings that the DMCA had left even lawful buyers unable to make fair uses of encrypted works [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Copyright owners — movie studios, record labels, and publishers — would lose the ability to charge separately for each copy, format, or device, and would lose the DRM-backed control that limits what buyers can do with purchases. The risk they would cite is increased piracy: easier copying and resale channels could cut into sales that fund the production of new music, films, and books.

drawbacks.text: Copyright owners argue that weakening DRM protections and permitting circumvention tools could open the door to piracy, since the same tools used for personal backups can be used for mass copying — a cost that could ultimately reduce the supply of new creative works [S2][S3].

The circumvention provision depends on a judgment call about when a copyright owner has 'failed' to accommodate a noninfringing use, which could invite litigation and uncertainty for device makers and online services [S2][S3].

Digital first sale is hard to police in practice: verifying that a seller truly deleted their copy and that the work stayed in its original format would require monitoring that raises its own costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer gains are real and familiar — the bill largely would have restored to digital purchases the rights people always had with books and CDs. The genuine trade-off is that easier copying and resale of perfect digital duplicates could erode sales, and the bill's enforcement lines (when circumvention is allowed, when a resold copy must be deleted) are blurry and would have required courts to draw them. The design tries to limit piracy by conditioning circumvention on the copyright owner's failure to accommodate legitimate uses, but critics would still worry about leakage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its intellectual property subcommittee in May 2003, and it sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Zoe Lofgren introduced the bill on March 4, 2003, joined by Rick Boucher, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
It drew six cosponsors — four Democrats and two Republicans — giving it small bipartisan support [S4].
On May 5, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property, where it remained with no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Movie studios, record labels, and publishers kept full legal and technological control over how consumers use digital purchases, and consumers gained nothing. The outcome preserved the status quo for the copyright industries at the cost of the rights the bill would have restored.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — six cosponsors split four Democrats and two Republicans — and it was never voted on, so no roll-call shows where parties stood; the outcome was determined by committee inaction rather than a recorded vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Movie studios, record labels, and publishers
industries.note: The bill would have weakened DRM-based control and license terms these industries use to charge for each format, device, and use of a digital work, and would have allowed circumvention for legitimate uses. Their revenue model of controlling post-purchase use was directly at stake.

The bill's device-transfer and circumvention provisions would have freed manufacturers to build players and software that move or play legally purchased digital works without infringement liability. Consumers and these firms would have won together.

Digital first sale and a safe path around DRM for noninfringing uses would have expanded lawful markets in digital resale and media services. The bill was framed as restoring balance the DMCA upset for the tech sector as much as for consumers.
